content.subject: Basic Electrical Engineering
content.topic: Energy Consumption and the Kilowatt-hour Concept
content.hook: Does ten bulbs for one hour consume more power than one for ten?
content.question: A 100-watt bulb runs for 10 hours, while ten 100-watt bulbs run for 1 hour. How does the total electrical energy consumed in each case compare?
options: One bulb consumes ten times more
Ten bulbs consume ten times more
One bulb consumes one hundred times more
content.answerLine: Both cases consume exactly the same energy.
explanation: Electrical energy is simply defined as the product of total electrical power consumed and operating time.
In standard engineering practice, the commercial unit of billing is the kilowatt-hour, equivalent to one Board of Trade unit.
For the first case, a single one-hundred-watt lamp operates steadily for a total duration of ten hours.
Multiplying one hundred watts by ten hours gives one thousand watt-hours, which equals exactly one kilowatt-hour.
content.funFact: One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 megajoules, which is enough energy to boil about ten litres of room-temperature water.
content.outro: Remember that energy integrates power over time, so share this quiz and follow for more engineering problems!

Running this one-kilowatt load for one hour yields one kilowatt multiplied by one hour of duration.
This product equals one kilowatt-hour, showing that energy integration over time yields identical numerical totals.
